content.text: How long does the Sun have left? It’s like life expectancy. I don’t know exactly when I’ll die — but based on statistics, an Australian woman is likely to live into her mid-80s. Astronomers do the same thing with stars. We’ve studied billions of stars and mapped them on what’s called the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram. About 90% sit on a diagonal band called the main sequence, meaning stars spend roughly 90% of their lives there. A star’s lifetime depends on two things: ✨ How much mass (fuel) it has ✨ How fast it burns that fuel (its luminosity) Think of it like a bank account. Hydrogen is the savings. Luminosity is the spending rate. Using Einstein’s E = mc², we can calculate how much energy is stored in the Sun’s hydrogen. Stellar models show the Sun will “go broke” after converting about 10% of its hydrogen into helium. When we divide the total available energy by how fast it’s being spent, we get its nuclear lifetime: about 10 billion years. The Sun formed about 5 billion years ago — confirmed by stellar physics and the ages of the oldest meteorites. So we’re roughly halfway through. About 5 billion years to go.
